    Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M.
    • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
    • Sources indicate that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

    Sources indicate that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

    The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

    In a recent development, “The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition indicates.

    In a recent development, trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

    In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

    In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

    Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

    The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

    The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a newly introduced removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

    Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

    A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

    Sources indicate that the case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

    The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

    The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

    • Sources indicate that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    Sources indicate that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that after that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    Recent findings suggest that now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it indicates this:.

    According to recent reports, not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    Sources indicate that so it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Recent findings suggest that then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary indicates something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    Recent findings suggest that as of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

    #88823. The Mid-Size Florida Hub Betting $1.5 Billion That Delta Air Lines Will Turn It Into An International Gateway

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1520 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Mid-Size Florida Hub Betting $1.5 Billion That Delta Air Lines Will Turn It Into An International Gateway

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age.
    • Tampa International Airport (TPA) is building a $1.528 billion terminal that will add 16 gates, a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area for international arrivals, and enough capacity to handle 35 million annual passengers by 2037.
    • In a recent development, delta signed a 20-year anchor lease for at least six of those gates, including a purpose-built Delta Sky Club lounge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

    Tampa International Airport (TPA) is building a $1.528 billion terminal that will add 16 gates, a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area for international arrivals, and enough capacity to handle 35 million annual passengers by 2037. Structural steel will begin going up this Summer, with completion targeted for late 2028 and a public opening in 2029. It is the airport's first fresh airside terminal in nearly 20 years.

    In a recent development, delta signed a 20-year anchor lease for at least six of those gates, including a purpose-built Delta Sky Club lounge. The commitment is the longest and most substantial terminal agreement Delta has made at any mid-size Florida airport. It positions Tampa as a potential international gateway for the airline once the new Federal Inspection Services facility gives the airport the processing capacity to support widebody international arrivals.

    TPA is building its first upcoming airside terminal in nearly 20 years. The Hillsborough County Aviation Authority Board approved the 100% final design for Airside D on February 5, clearing the project for full construction. The facility will be 600,000 square feet (55,742 sq meters) with 16 gates serving both domestic and international flights.

    It includes a latest Federal Inspection Services area for processing international arrivals, an 8-lane security checkpoint, and a new checked baggage inspection system in the main terminal. The total project cost is $1.528 billion, including a $902 million supplemental contract approved in late 2025.

    Construction is well underway. A 300-ton crane is erecting the structural steel framework, which consists of 6,200 tons of steel comprising over 7,300 individual pieces connected by 96,000 bolts and 212,000 inches of welding. Approximately 200 workers are on site daily, with that number expected to increase significantly as the project moves from structural work into mechanical, electrical, and interior fit-out phases.

    In a recent development, HNTB designed the project, the same firm that designed TPA's existing main terminal and automated people mover system. Completion is targeted for late 2028 with a public opening in 2029. Once operational, Airside D will increase TPA's total gate count and expand the airport's annual passenger capacity from its current 25 million to 35 million by 2037.

    Industry observers note that the airport handled approximately 24 million passengers in 2024, meaning it is approaching the capacity limits of its existing terminal complex. Airside D provides the infrastructure to accommodate the growth TPA has been experiencing without the crowding and gate constraints that would otherwise limit airline expansion at the airport.

    Industry observers note that delta was selected as the anchor tenant for Airside D in a decision unveiled by the Hillsborough County Aviation Authority. The lease covers at least six of the 16 gates on a 20-year term, giving Delta a dedicated presence in the fresh facility through approximately 2049. The agreement includes a mezzanine-level Delta Sky Club, the carrier's first purpose-built lounge at TPA.

    It has been revealed that the remaining 10 gates will be available for other carriers, with the airport authority retaining flexibility to assign them based on demand and airline interest. A 20-year anchor lease at a mid-size airport is not a routine commitment. Delta operates from dozens of airports across the United States, but it signs long-term anchor agreements only at facilities where it intends to build or sustain a significant operation over multiple decades.

    In a recent development, the lease term matches the terminal's useful life, meaning Delta is committing to Tampa for as long as Airside D operates. The Sky Club inclusion signals that Delta expects enough premium traffic at TPA to justify the capital investment and ongoing operating cost of a dedicated lounge, which the airline typically reserves for its largest hubs and busiest focus cities.

    According to recent reports, delta currently operates approximately 45 daily departures from Tampa to destinations including Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis-St. Paul, Salt Lake City, Upcoming York-JFK, Boston, and Amsterdam. The Amsterdam route, operated on the A330-900, is Delta's first year-round widebody international service from TPA.

    It serves as a proof of concept for the kind of European flying the airline could expand from Airside D once the facility opens. The six-gate commitment in a terminal with a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area positions Delta to add additional international routes from Tampa without competing for gate space or customs processing capacity in the airport's existing international facility.

    Industry observers note that delta operates the largest domestic hub-and-spoke network of any US carrier. It is built around hubs at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta Airport (ATL), Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC), Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    It has been revealed that atlanta is the largest by a wide margin, handling over 1,000 daily Delta departures and serving as the airline's primary connecting hub for domestic and international traffic. Delta's existing Florida footprint is substantial but spread across multiple airports without a dominant hub presence at any single one.

    The airline operates from Orlando International Airport (MCO), Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Miami International Airport (MIA), Jacksonville International Airport (JAX), and TPA, among others. None of those airports functions as a Delta hub in the way that Atlanta or Detroit do.

    Industry observers note that however, Orlando and Fort Lauderdale carry the highest Florida frequencies, driven by leisure demand from Delta's Northeastern and Midwestern hubs. The anchor tenant commitment does not make Tampa a hub. Delta is not building a connecting operation at TPA comparable to what it runs at Atlanta or Detroit.

    According to recent reports, the lease establishes Tampa as a long-term focus city with dedicated infrastructure, a premium lounge, and the physical capacity to grow well beyond the 45 daily departures Delta right now operates. The distinction matters because a focus city with a 20-year lease and a purpose-built Sky Club receives a different level of investment and scheduling priority than a station where the airline operates from shared gates on short-term agreements.

    TPA already handles international flights. Edelweiss serves Zurich, Avianca recently introduced daily service to Bogota, and Delta added year-round Amsterdam service. Caribbean and Canadian routes to destinations including San Juan, Toronto, Montreal, Cancun, and Santo Domingo operate from the existing terminal.

    Industry observers note that the airport is not starting international service from zero. What it lacks is the capacity to grow it meaningfully beyond what the current Federal Inspection Services facility can process. Airside D's dedicated FIS area changes that constraint. The new facility will have its own Customs and Border Protection processing area capable of handling widebody international arrivals simultaneously with domestic operations on the same concourse.

    Delta's six gates in a terminal with FIS capability give the airline the infrastructure to operate international flights from Tampa without competing for processing capacity in the airport's existing international arrivals facility. Routes to London, Paris, or additional European destinations that require a full international arrivals hall become operationally feasible in a way they are not today from Delta's current gate positions.

    The most striking figure in the airport authority's route development materials is the leakage rate. Approximately 50% of Tampa's international origin-and-destination traffic at the moment uses other Florida airports, primarily MIA, MCO, and FLL.

    Recent findings suggest that tampa Bay area residents flying internationally drive to other airports because nonstop international options from TPA are limited. Airside D's FIS capacity, combined with Delta's anchor presence and the gate infrastructure to support widebody international service, is designed to recapture that leakage by giving Tampa the facilities to offer the international routes its local market already demands.

    Recent findings suggest that the Tampa Bay metropolitan area is one of the fastest-growing regions in the US. The four-county metro area comprising Hillsborough, Pinellas, Pasco, and Hernando counties has added over 400,000 residents since 2010 and now exceeds 3.3 million people. The region's economy has diversified beyond its traditional tourism and military base.

    Sources indicate that indeed, the finance, healthcare, technology, and logistics sectors are driving corporate travel demand alongside the leisure traffic that has historically defined Florida aviation. TPA handled 24.5 million passengers in fiscal year 2025, approaching the 25 million capacity ceiling the airport authority identified as the trigger point for Airside D.

    The 2029 opening timing aligns with several fleet developments at Delta. Namely, Delta's Airbus A350-1000 deliveries will begin in late 2026, freeing up A330-900s and A350-900s that could be deployed on international routes from secondary hubs and focus cities, including Tampa.

    Delta's year-round Amsterdam service, launched on the A330-900, is a proof of concept for European widebody service from TPA. If the route performs well through 2027 and 2028, additional European destinations from Airside D's gates become a natural extension of the strategy once the facility opens.

    In a recent development, rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

    Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

    Sources indicate that the red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

    Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

    Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

    A newcomer to electoral politics, she rapidly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

    In a recent development, in 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

    It has been revealed that running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

    According to recent reports, this year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

    Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

    Breaking: Lockheed’s CL-1201 Was A Nuclear-Powered Flying Aircraft Carrier That Never Left The Drawing Board

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the early jet era, Lockheed had a full docket of pioneering aerospace programs, but even among the iconic airplanes in the Skunk Works portfolio, the CL-1201 stands out for its scale and ambition.
    • It was a nearly 6,000-ton (5,375 metric tons) flying wing that spanned 1,120 feet (341 meters) in an audacious technical leap to rewrite strategic air mobility and power projection over foreign soil.
    • Sources indicate that although the aerodynamics and physics of constructing such a flying colossus sound like the greatest technical hurdle to its success, the failure of its nuclear power source stopped any progress.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the early jet era, Lockheed had a full docket of pioneering aerospace programs, but even among the iconic airplanes in the Skunk Works portfolio, the CL-1201 stands out for its scale and ambition. Locked in the endlessly escalating arms race with the Soviet Union, the US Air Force has commissioned an engineering study into a flying, nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. On September 12, 1969, Lockheed engineers G. Daniel Brewer, S. Dalton, and P. J. Sibley filed a organization report LR-22802, outlining a machine that seemed to defy physics.

    It was a nearly 6,000-ton (5,375 metric tons) flying wing that spanned 1,120 feet (341 meters) in an audacious technical leap to rewrite strategic air mobility and power projection over foreign soil. The mothership was expected to haul at least 22 McDonnell Douglas fighter jets on massive underwing pylons in the same way that the smaller planes carried missiles. Designated the CL-1201, the behemoth 'lightning' carrier would be capable of reaching any conflict zone in hours and promised to cruise for 41 straight days without resupply.

    Sources indicate that although the aerodynamics and physics of constructing such a flying colossus sound like the greatest technical hurdle to its success, the failure of its nuclear power source stopped any progress. Popular accounts of the program claim that the USAF did in fact commission an active service example. However, no records to date, including the most detailed public file NASA, recorded as Memorandum X-2386, show that any order was officially lodged.

    The CL-1201's propulsion abandoned standard jet fuel logistics in favor of an unproven liquid-metal-cooled reactor delivering 1,830 megawatts of thermal energy. That staggering heat drove four mammoth aft turbofans at Mach 0.8 at 30,000 feet (9,144 meters), offering effectively unlimited global range. The design aimed to bypass the need for any overseas airfields and reliance on allied partners entirely by maintaining an airborne presence for over a month, limited only by crew endurance and engine oil.

    The primary CL-1201-1-1 Attack Aircraft Carrier variant would house a crew of 845 to operate 22 fighters beneath its wings. Meanwhile, the alternative CL-1201-1-3 Logistics Support Aircraft traded strike fighters for a cavernous cargo bay. It was proposed with the capacity to deploy an entire combat brigade of 3,896 soldiers with 6,207 tons (5,631 metric tons) of equipment to any hot spot on the globe.

    In a recent development, eight years before Lockheed's engineers filed their report, US President John F. Kennedy had already canceled the US aircraft nuclear propulsion program. After 15 years of research, it was finally called off in 1961. The numbers had never successfully solved all the safety issues with installing an active nuclear reactor in an airplane. Two airships, the USS Akron and Macon, preceded the C-1201 as early motherships, and one Convair NB-36H had been equipped with nuclear power plants for test flights.

    Industry observers note that yet, scientists were unable to ever create an atomic engine considered safe enough to not have a devastating environmental impact in the event of a mishap. Furthermore, turning the CL-1201 concept into an airworthy airframe demanded solving the immediate physics problem of how to lift nearly 12 million lb (5.4 million kg) into the sky. No airport on Earth could handle the landing gear footprint, forcing the design team to adopt a complex propulsion compromise.

    The retrieval system of the CL-1201 lowered a hydraulically stabilized pantograph hook 35 feet (10.7 meters) beneath the airframe into clean, undisturbed air. A docking fighter pilot engaged the hook with a dorsal latch, allowing heavy winches to haul the aircraft up against cradle stops before swinging it into internal maintenance bays. This acrobatic aerial recovery demanded precision flying in high-altitude crosswinds, turning routine combat patrols into dangerous flight-test maneuvers that risked pilot lives.

    Docking a 40,000-lb (18,140 kg) fighter beneath a 125,000-square-foot (11,613 sq m) wing generated lethal aerodynamic turbulence that tested the limits of human piloting. Incoming flight crews had to fly through a violent boundary layer wake and wingtip vortex wash, with velocity spikes exceeding 120 feet (37 meters) per second. The chaotic upwash threatened to smash approaching jets against the lower wing skin, prompting designers to engineer an articulated trapeze boom.

    According to recent reports, beyond the docking challenges, Cold War missile advances made the carrier extraordinarily vulnerable to long-range Soviet surface-to-air missile networks. The tailless 560-foot (171-meter) airframe would look like staring into the sun on an enemy's radar scope. Its gigantic profile would create an immense radar target that air defense systems like the Soviet S-200 Angara could spot hundreds of miles away. A single missile strike could instantly wipe out an entire combat wing and crack open the central atomic reactor.

    At a gross weight of 11.85 million lb (5.4 million kg), roughly fifteen times the mass of a Boeing 747 or Lockheed C-5 Galaxy, the CL-1201 exceeded the limits of every runway in the world. Standard concrete aprons would be crushed under its landing gear, while constructing dedicated five-mile runways around the world negated the strategic autonomy that justified it. To eliminate runway dependence, engineering lead Brewer and his team adopted an extreme vertical takeoff and landing design.

    It has been revealed that rather than routing reactor thermal energy to lift fans, the configuration housed 182 dedicated jet-fuel-powered turbojets in retractable forward fuselage bays and inner wing banks. It would dramatically scale up the multi-engine vertical lift concept of experimental aircraft at the time, like the Dornier Do 31 and Yakovlev Yak 38. Each turbine was rated for 90,000 pounds of thrust for a combined vertical output of 16.38 million pounds.

    In operational practice, this propulsion created severe liabilities at every launch site. Simultaneous ignition of 182 lift jets projected a 1,400°F downward exhaust plume capable of spalling reinforced concrete, liquefying asphalt, and generating severe foreign object damage hazards across massive areas. Furthermore, the lift engines would consume nearly 1.9 million lb (0.8 million kg) of JP-5 fuel during a single five-minute departure sequence, burning the equivalent fuel capacity of six fully loaded C-5 Galaxies before the nuclear engines engaged.

    Additionally, synchronizing 182 independent turbines during the low-speed transition from jet-borne hover to wing-borne aerodynamic flight introduced an alarmingly long list of potential failure points. A compressor stall or flameout within an outboard wing bank would generate violent asymmetric roll moments far exceeding the control authority of aerodynamic flight surfaces at near-zero airspeed. Ultimately, the CL 1201 was simply unviable due to its inability to break away from conventional infrastructure and limitations because of its size and not its power source, relegating the concept to a Cold War 'flight of fancy.'.

    Recent findings suggest that in the 1940s and 1950s, the USAF and Atomic Energy Commission spent roughly $1 billion over 15 years on the Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion (ANP) program, hoping to build bombers that could stay airborne for weeks. The Convair NB-36H Crusader flew 47 test missions over Texas and New Mexico carrying an operational, air-cooled 1-to-3 megawatt reactor in its aft bomb bay. The bomber's entire nose had a 12-ton lead and rubber shield, complete with 12-inch-thick lead-glass windows.

    Adding the 17.5-ton reactor meant the aircraft had to haul nearly 30 tons of nuclear hardware and shielding before carrying any weapons. Every test flight was shadowed by a C-97 transport plane carrying a platoon of US Marines trained to parachute into the crash site and cordon off radioactive debris. Engineers could not solve the dilemma of making a reactor light enough without sacrificing containment. Furthermore, advances in intercontinental ballistic missiles and aerial refueling made nuclear bombers strategically obsolete.

    Industry observers note that lockheed aimed to overcome those limitations with an atomic propulsion plant rated at an astonishing 5,470 megawatts in a dual-circuit closed loop. Liquid lithium circulated through the primary reactor core at temperatures reaching 2,000°F (1,093°C), carrying thermal energy into an intermediate heat exchanger mounted inside a central structural containment cell. The secondary circuit circulated non-radioactive liquid alloy through pipes to four massive trailing-edge turbofans.

    In a recent development, the engines used single-stage titanium fan disks spanning an unprecedented 28 feet (8.5 meters) across. The liquid metal radiators sat directly behind the 14-stage axial compressors, transferring heat into the compressed air stream to produce 300,000 pounds of thrust (1,334 kN) per engine. Containing the energy required a titanium keel and trusses that were eight inches (20 cm) thick, as well as a shield of lead, tungsten, and borated water weighing 1.2 million lb (544,300 kg).

    Commissioned in the early 1930s, the USS Akron (ZRS-4) and her sister ship USS Macon (ZRS-5) were 785-foot-long rigid helium airships. Each airship housed an internal hangar bay holding up to five Curtiss F9C-2 Sparrowhawk biplanes. To launch, a mechanical 'trapeze' lowered a fighter beneath the airship's hull into the slipstream, where the pilot released a skyhook and flew away. To recover, the pilot matched the airship's 70-knot speed and snagged the trapeze bar with a hook mounted above the upper wing.

    Industry observers note that on April 4, 1933, the Akron was caught in a violent thunderstorm off the coast of New Jersey. Downdrafts forced the tail into the Atlantic Ocean, breaking the airship apart. Less than two years later, on February 12, 1935, the Macon encountered a storm off Point Sur, California. Wind shear tore away her upper tail fin, puncturing rear gas cells and causing her to lose buoyancy and settle into the Pacific.

    In a recent development, before the tragic and catastrophic demise of each airship, the trapeze system actually worked well, and the Navy never lost a plane during an in-flight catch. Despite successful fighter operations, the loss of the Macon ended the US Navy's permanent pursuit of flying aircraft carriers, and there's no indication that they ever revealed interest in the massive Lockheed concept. Meanwhile, the CL-1201 aimed to take this ill-fated earlier attempt and supersize it.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard.
    • This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service challenges at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

    This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service challenges at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a latest initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

    According to recent reports, emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

    Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a latest initiative involving this small group of employees:.

    On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

    This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

    So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

    A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

    Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

    For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

    According to recent reports, it goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

    Sources indicate that when it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

    As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

    I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

    Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

    Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

    There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

    #88813. Why United Airlines Is The Only US Carrier Left With An Overseas Hub

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1525 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why United Airlines Is The Only US Carrier Left With An Overseas Hub

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that in general, the US legacy carriers primarily operate their networks within the continental US.
    • United currently operates up to 12 daily flights to 15 different destinations in five countries out of Guam Antonio B.
    • Industry observers note that in 1968, Continental Airlines and regional shareholders established Air Micronesia, initially headquartered in the Northern Mariana Islands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in general, the US legacy carriers primarily operate their networks within the continental US. All of American Airlines' ten hub airports are located within the continental US, as are all of Delta's nine hub airports. United Airlines, however, has seven hub airports in the continental US, as well as a hub in Guam, an overseas territory of the US located thousands of miles away from Washington. It's the only such operation by any US airline, and it carries on the legacy of an operation that goes back nearly 60 years.

    United currently operates up to 12 daily flights to 15 different destinations in five countries out of Guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM). It is the start/end for the carrier's famous 'Island Hopper' service, and the airline also runs direct services from GUM to San Francisco with a stopover in Honolulu. This route uses a Boeing 777-300ER, while the rest of the GUM routes use the Boeing 737. United is by far the largest airline serving Guam, and it also serves as a vital link connecting Guam to the outside world.

    Industry observers note that in 1968, Continental Airlines and regional shareholders established Air Micronesia, initially headquartered in the Northern Mariana Islands. Operating under the callsign 'Air Mike', the airline initially operated Boeing 727s and became a crucial component in the region's economic development during the late 20th century. Air Micronesia held a near monopoly in the market, and its 727s were crucial in connecting what were previously remote islands to the outside world.

    In a recent development, continental would eventually own 100% of Air Micronesia, rebranding the airline to 'Continental Micronesia' while the headquarters eventually shifted to Guam. While other airlines attempted to connect Guam to the US at certain points and others served Micronesia from foreign countries, Continental Micronesia was by far the largest airline in this market. Among its most famous routes was the 'Island Hopper', connecting Guam to Honolulu with five stopovers, and the airline also had a substantial international network.

    In 1999, Continental Micronesia began transitioning from using the 727 to the 737NG for most operations, and in 2003, the Guam International Airport Facility pushed commuter airlines out of GUM's Commuter Terminal and leased the facility to Continental. The airline would become Guam's largest private-sector employer, while connecting GUM to over 20 destinations.

    It has been revealed that in 2010, Continental Airlines unveiled that it would merge with United Airlines, keeping the United name. In 2017, Continental Micronesia was formally merged into United Airlines (it had previously operated as a subsidiary of United Continental Holdings), and today, all Guam flights are directly operated by United.

    According to recent reports, airlines are hardly afraid of shutting down unprofitable hubs, and United itself dehubbed the Cleveland hub that it also inherited from Continental during the merger in 2014. However, the Guam operations were making money for the airline, and they're a vital link to the communities served. In addition, United absolutely dominates Guam, and the hub offers a unique strategic position within the carrier's network that couldn't otherwise be replicated by another hub.

    According to recent reports, guam itself is a hub for lucrative military and government activity, and United's position in Guam means that it essentially receives all government travel contracts. Because of the airline's dominance in GUM, it can also charge high fares due to the lack of competition. Altogether, Guam is actually one of United's most lucrative hubs, even if it is also one of its smallest. The operation makes the airline money, and so it will remain a United hub, even as other US legacy carriers have dehubbed their hubs outside of the US mainland.

    Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Denver International Airport (DEN).

    Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

    According to recent reports, guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM).

    San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

    Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

    Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

    According to recent reports, in March 2026, the carrier began transitioning from using the 737-800 to the 737 MAX 8 for its Guam operations, with the switch having been completed in October. These ten aircraft feature a significantly upgraded interior compared to the old 737-800s, and they feature signs in English and Japanese rather than English and Spanish, while the front row of economy can be collapsed to accommodate a stretcher for medevac flights. In addition, two United First seats are blocked on the Island Hopper to be used as a pilot crew rest facility.

    It has been revealed that going into the 2010s, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines both operated hubs at Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT). These hubs had operated for decades (Delta inherited NRT operations from Northwest Airlines, while United acquired the NRT routes from Pan Am) and essentially connected US passengers to Asia, serving as a central hub. But in the mid-2010s, United gradually discontinued intra-Asia routes out of NRT, and Delta exited NRT entirely in 2020 (it will return in 2027 with a single route from Seattle).

    Recent findings suggest that whereas United's Guam hub primarily serves the local market, the NRT hubs operated by United and Delta mainly existed for connections. However, the arrival of the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 allowed these airlines to serve more destinations in Asia nonstop from the US, and nonstop flights typically earn a fare premium over one-stop options. As such, the NRT hubs weren't necessary anymore, since they were essentially set up due to range limitations of older widebodies like the Boeing 747-200.

    In addition to the improved economics of new widebody aircraft, United revealed a joint venture with All Nippon Airways in 2011, while Delta announced a joint venture with Korean Air in 2017. With these, the intra-Asia routes are covered by their joint venture partners, eliminating the need to operate these flights with their own metal. In other words, United's NRT hub has been replaced by nonstop flights to Asia and ANA's operations out of Tokyo, while Delta's NRT hub has been replaced by Korean Air's hub in Seoul.

    Industry observers note that apart from the carrier's one-stop flight from GUM to San Francisco via Honolulu with the 777-300ER, all of United's Guam routes now use the 737 MAX 8. There are currently ten of them stationed in GUM, and they operate to Taipei, Manila, Airai, Saipan, Yap, Pohnpei, Chuuk, Tokyo Narita, Tokyo Haneda, Osaka, and Nagoya. In addition, the airline's flight to Airai continues to Manila on some days of the week, while the flight to Chuuk is part of the Island Hopper, flying from Guam to Honolulu via Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, Kwajalein, and Majuro.

    Several of these routes do not operate daily, as local demand is ultimately limited and the 737 MAX 8 is a relatively large aircraft, able to carry up to 166 passengers in United's configuration. Japan is United's largest market out of GUM, as it connects the airport to four airports in Japan while operating up to five daily flights between GUM and Japan. Notably, United does not serve Nagoya from the mainland US nonstop.

    Sources indicate that some of these routes can be extremely long, which makes the fuel savings of the 737 MAX 8 over the 737-800 highly impactful. Meanwhile, the 777-300ER is flown to Guam almost entirely due to strong demand for cargo, as this is the aircraft in United's fleet with the highest cargo capacity. The airline only has 22 of these planes, which make up less than 10% of its overall widebody fleet, and yet the cargo revenue is strong enough to justify its use on the San Francisco-Honolulu-Guam route.

    While United's Guam operations have generally been successful, the hub has been facing difficulties in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as a decline in demand from Japan, the largest market for the hub. Ordinarily, United may simply shift capacity to another hub, but that isn't easy to do with Guam. The airport is thousands of miles away from any of United's other hubs, the carrier has a pilot and flight attendant base in Guam, and the ten 737s are specially configured for these services.

    What United has done with these assets is move them back to NRT. In recent years, the carrier has released upcoming fifth freedom routes from NRT to Cebu, Kaohsiung, and Ulaanbaatar, using the flight numbers of the carrier's nonstop flights to NRT from the mainland US and operating the flights with Guam-based 737s. Crucially, these destinations are not served by ANA, which means that United is expanding the joint venture's Asia coverage while deploying assets that would have otherwise been underutilized.

    In a recent development, it's one of the most creative ways to utilize assets when the standard operation is no longer producing the returns that it once did. Not only that, but the airline has generated tremendous excitement and publicity over these routes, with the Ulaanbaatar route standing out in particular, and this is beneficial for loyalty program and credit card sign-ups, which is where the carrier makes its real money.

    Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1479 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I promptly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I promptly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    Sources indicate that I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    It has been revealed that I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    Sources indicate that as the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and indicated the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically mentioned, “that means nothing.”.

    Industry observers note that so they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Recent findings suggest that only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a significant deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    Industry observers note that airline loyalty is really crucial to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    Sources indicate that that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    In a recent development, back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    It has been revealed that even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    In a recent development, inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    It has been revealed that it was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    Sources indicate that it’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of upcoming Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    It has been revealed that if I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

    Breaking: Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that former Rep.
    • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family unveiled.
    • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

    Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family unveiled.

    In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

    As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

    In a recent development, “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

    When McDermott confirmed his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

    Industry observers note that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

    In a recent development, he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

    He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against newly introduced sanctions on Iran.

    Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

    According to recent reports, “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

    As he noted, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

    Sources indicate that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

    “The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

    It has been revealed that mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

    In a recent development, “Jim McDermott was as significant as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

    Industry News: End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore.
    • As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.
    • Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

    As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

    Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with latest cabins, including the new business class.

    Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

    In a recent development, with this change, no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore either, so it very much is the end of an era. American’s 777 first class seats were controversial — on the one hand, I kind of love how they swivel, though on the other hand, they really lack privacy, and the soft product left a lot to be desired.

    I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

    It’s great that these planes will be getting upcoming business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

    While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

    Sources indicate that specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between Fresh York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

    American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

    American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

    American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

    In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

    What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
    • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

    The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

    He noted “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

    During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

    In a recent development, earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from latest software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin remarked “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

    Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

    According to recent reports, “This is an emergency,” he stated. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

    The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

    Mullin mentioned the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

    “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

    Sources indicate that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

    Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

    Sources indicate that senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

    Industry observers note that the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

    The committee’s majority mentioned Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a latest one was built.

    Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., remarked in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications challenges.

    “Technology complications related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

    Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

    In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

    Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

    Industry observers note that at issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have stated they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.
